case_study_insert.main_stem: Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative (SBV) is a cooperative owned by 31 member grape-growing families in the wine production sector, employing a workforce of 58. Founded in 1994 and led by chairperson Tessa Vidal, the cooperative vinifies member grapes into single-vineyard still and sparkling wines sold to independent wine merchants and its cellar door, operating a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership among member growers. SBV plans to invest $950,000 in a temperature-controlled fermentation and barrel-maturation hall with an extended cellar door and online shop, financed by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.60 a unit and a selling price of $16.80, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. SBV faces two problems: labour turnover among casual harvest pickers reached 28% this season, and barrel-fault defect rates are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Cellar Operations Log — Q3 2026: The winery crushed 310 tonnes of member grapes last vintage. Bottle-fault inspections found a defect rate of 2.1% (cork taint and fill faults), down from 3.0% a year ago. Complaints from wine merchants fell from 19 to 9 per month. Average dispatch time is 5.5 days. A survey of 800 wine buyers found that 59% would pay up to $1.20 more for single-vineyard co-op wine, and 51% check sustainable viticulture certification before buying. The board is weighing a $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus to retain casual harvest pickers, and it is deciding between permanent cellar positions and seasonal casual contracts for the coming vintage; casual pickers averaged 34 hours a week this year.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for vineyard equipment finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $13.45 to $14.38 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills for casual harvest staff working 34 hours a week. (3) Bottle glass and cork costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, and wine inflation is running at 8.3%, while consumer spending on premium wine grew 3.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SBV plans to fund the fermentation hall with $550,000 retained profit and a $400,000 community share issue. Explain two advantages for SBV of using retained profit instead of relying entirely on the community share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs SBV nothing in dividends, interest or issue administration, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative whose 31 member families already expect stable grape payments while it funds a $950,000 hall. Avoiding sole reliance on the community share issue reduces the risk that member appetite for shares falls short of the target, which would leave the fermentation hall underfunded or push SBV toward expensive unplanned borrowing from a bank that knows nothing of wine cycles — damaging member confidence in the cooperative model itself.

Point 2: Using retained profit first signals to members and wine merchants that SBV is financially disciplined and self-reliant, strengthening confidence in the single-vineyard expansion and in the 59% premium-willing segment identified in its research. It also preserves the $400,000 community share issue as a buffer for cost overruns on the temperature-controlled hall — significant because barrel-fault defects and 13.2% bottle-glass inflation could both squeeze the project's budget before the 2027 vintage, and because member appetites for further share calls would fade if the hall overran its cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Stonebarrow Vineyard & Wine Co-operative and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: SBV is launching its single-vineyard co-op range of still and sparkling wines. Consider cellar-door wine-tasting events, targeted social media advertising, or local radio sponsorship. Which should SBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Cellar-door wine-tasting events: Tasting events at the cellar door let visitors sample the single-vineyard range, meet the member growers and buy direct, deepening loyalty and supporting the $16.80 price point without wine-merchant margin. They showcase the 51% of buyers who check sustainable viticulture certification with face-to-face storytelling. The limitation is capacity: the cellar door already serves visitors while handling dispatch in 5.5 days, so tastings can never reach buyers beyond the local region, and each event sells limited volume relative to a 120,000-unit annual output target.

Targeted social media advertising: Targeted campaigns on food, wine and lifestyle channels can reach precisely the 59% of 800 surveyed buyers willing to pay up to $1.20 more for single-vineyard co-op wine, across every region and export market the online shop serves, with measurable click-through to the shop and retargeting of engagers. It costs a fraction of mass media, fits SBV's cooperative, low-overheads ethos, and can feature member-grower stories and certification badges — though it demands regular content and results build over weeks rather than instantly.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio delivers frequency and name recall in the immediate region at low cost, and a harvest-time sponsorship slot would reach loyal local wine drinkers effectively. However, radio cannot target premium wine buyers specifically, much of its audience neither visits the cellar door nor orders online, and coverage stops at the transmitter boundary while SBV ships to independent merchants across multiple regions.

Recommendation: SBV should choose targeted social media advertising. It alone combines precise targeting of the 59% premium-willing segment and the 51% certification-checkers, national scalability for the online shop, measurable returns on the $950,000 investment, and low cost suited to a cooperative without large marketing reserves. Cellar-door tastings are rejected as the lead strategy because their limited local reach cannot move 120,000 units a year; local radio is rejected as untargeted and geographically capped, though one monthly tasting evening should continue as a complement rather than the anchor of the launch campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SBV with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SBV with a well-justified recommendation explaining why cellar-door events and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: SBV's labour turnover among casual harvest pickers reached 28% this season. Explain two benefits for SBV of using a harvest bonus to motivate pickers during the vintage.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A harvest bonus tied to tonnes picked gives casual pickers a direct financial incentive to stay for the whole crush rather than leave mid-vintage, directly attacking the 28% turnover. Because the bonus scales with output, SBV pays only for results — crucial when pickers work 34 hours a week and the winery crushed 310 tonnes of member grapes that must be processed within days of picking.

Point 2: A completion bonus at the end of harvest raises morale and loyalty beyond the picking rows, making pickers more willing to return next year and to handle fruit carefully — which supports the 2.1% bottle-fault defect target and the falling complaints from 19 to 9 per month. Retaining experienced pickers also cuts re-recruitment and induction costs and protects member growers' fruit quality, reinforcing the cooperative's democratic values and member confidence in Tessa Vidal's leadership — while giving seasonal workers a tangible reason to return for the 2027 vintage.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SBV's labour turnover, vintage workload and defect rate.

questions.question_text: SBV needs reliable workers for the coming vintage. Consider offering permanent cellar positions or seasonal casual contracts. Which should SBV choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Permanent cellar positions: Permanent contracts would end the 28% labour turnover among pickers, give the winery a skilled core team that knows the temperature-controlled fermentation hall, barrel handling and bottle-fault standards, and support long-horizon quality gains such as pushing the 2.1% defect rate below 2%. Permanent staff also justify off-the-job training investment, answer member growers' demands for consistency, and are easier to brief on the sustainable viticulture certification that 51% of buyers check. The downsides are higher fixed wage costs through quiet months — pickers work only seasonally on current 34-hour weeks — plus redundancy risk if a vintage fails, and permanent employment law obligations such as employment contracts and redundancy processes that a small cooperative must administer.

Seasonal casual contracts: Seasonal contracts scale labour to the crush exactly when it is needed, keep fixed costs low, preserve flexibility in lean years, and suit pickers who only want vintage work; they also protect cash ahead of the $950,000 hall investment and match the proposed $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus. However, they entrench the 28% turnover, require retraining every season, risk inconsistent fruit handling and higher defects, and undermine the certification credibility and merchant relationships SBV is building for its single-vineyard range.

Decision: SBV should offer permanent cellar positions for a core team of cellar and bottling staff, keeping seasonal casual contracts only for the peak crush weeks with the harvest bonus attached. Permanent contracts solve the root cause — 28% turnover — protect quality in the new hall, and are affordable against $950,000-expansion economics since cellar work continues year-round; pure seasonal contracting is rejected because it recreates the very churn, defect and retraining costs SBV must eliminate to supply premium merchants, would weaken the certification story, and would leave member growers' fruit handling expertise walking away every autumn.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of permanent and seasonal employment with limited application to SBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of both options in the context of SBV's labour turnover and vintage workload.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of SBV with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, retention and certification credibility.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SBV's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($16.80 − $9.60) = $360,000 ÷ $7.20 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.80 − $9.60 = $7.20. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.20.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SBV's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SBV's board can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 120,000 units to confirm the cooperative is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 70,000 units, which supports approving the $950,000 fermentation and maturation hall without endangering member payments.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.20 lets SBV model merchant price negotiations and the $1.20 premium: managers can test whether the 59% premium-willing segment sustains a $18.00 price, lifting contribution to $8.40, before committing to larger print runs of member-grower-labelled bottles.
3. Fixed costs of $360,000 and contribution per unit allow the board to stress-test the $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit funding plan, verifying that interest-free member funding keeps contribution available for the 13.2% bottle-glass and cork inflation.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($360,000 ÷ 120,000 units + $9.60 = $12.60 a unit) to benchmark each vintage, quantify the cost of the 2.1% bottle-fault rate, and evaluate whether the proposed $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus is cheaper than replacing casual pickers at 28% turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.20 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 70,000 units against 120,000-unit output; premium-pricing modelling from $7.20 contribution; funding checks for the $950,000 hall financed by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.60 to reduce the 2.1% bottle-fault rate and the 28% picker turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SBV's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Which judgement do the figures support — has SBV's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.97 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.24 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $320,000 inventories + $210,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $590,000; 2025 current assets = $290,000 + $240,000 + $85,000 = $615,000. Short-term coverage 2024 = $590,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.97; 2025 = $615,000 ÷ $275,000 = 2.24. Quick coverage excluding inventories 2024 = ($590,000 − $320,000) ÷ $300,000 = $270,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.90; 2025 = ($615,000 − $290,000) ÷ $275,000 = $325,000 ÷ $275,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened further. The coverage of immediate obligations improved from 1.97 to 2.24, helped by current liabilities falling from $300,000 to $275,000 and cash rising to $85,000. The quick coverage improved from 0.90 to 1.18, so SBV no longer needs to draw down inventories to meet short-term debts — important while capital employed rises from $3,190,000 to $4,040,000 on the strength of the new hall funded by member shares and retained profit rather than new external debt. Two cautions remain: trade receivables rose from $210,000 to $240,000, meaning independent wine merchants are paying later, and inventories fell to $290,000, which is efficient but leaves a thinner stock buffer if the 2027 vintage underdelivers or barrel-fault defects force batch quarantine. The very high coverage also hints that SBV may hold cash more productively, for example by forward-buying bottle glass ahead of the 13.2% price rise.

Conclusion: SBV's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.97 to 2.24) and the acid test ratio (0.90 to 1.18) show healthier short-term solvency, liabilities have been repaid, and the quick coverage now clears 1.0 comfortably without depending on stock sales. SBV should nonetheless tighten merchant credit terms and ring-fence part of the community share issue proceeds against bottle-glass inflation before releasing remaining funds to the hall extension and online shop.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SBV's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SBV of introducing sustainable viticulture certification for its member vineyards.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Sustainable viticulture certification would activate the 51% of 800 surveyed buyers who already check certification before purchasing, letting SBV command the $1.20 single-vineyard premium from the 59% premium-willing segment and supporting its listings with independent wine merchants across every market the online shop serves. It also differentiates SBV's member growers from commodity producers, strengthens the cooperative's sustainability story behind the $950,000 hall, and can be printed on bottle labels and the cellar door's tasting notes at virtually no extra cost.

Disadvantage: Certification requires audit fees, vineyard record-keeping, possible limits on sprays and fertilisers, and sometimes lower yields in conversion years — all of which raise the $9.60 variable cost or squeeze the $360,000 fixed-cost base further. If member growers fail an audit, whole parcels could be declassified, damaging the single-vineyard reputation and the $16.80 price point; and certification does nothing by itself to reduce the 2.1% bottle-fault defect rate or the 28% picker turnover that are SBV's most urgent operational problems, so it should not divert cash needed for the barrel hall.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SBV's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in bottle glass and cork costs will affect SBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): SBV's $950,000 expansion is funded by a $400,000 community share issue and $550,000 retained profit, not new variable-rate debt, so the direct hit is small — it applies mainly to any equipment finance and overdraft margins; a 0.75-point rise on modest borrowing adds at most a few thousand dollars a year. It could, however, temper consumer premium spending if households trade down from $16.80 bottles, and it raises the minimum return the board expects when it tests future purchases such as replacement barrels or the online shop build-out.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $14.38 per hour): SBV employs 58 staff plus casual harvest pickers on 34-hour weeks. A 6.9% rise adds roughly $1,900 per full-time worker and increases the cost of the proposed $0.40-per-tonne harvest bonus scheme; for the casual picker cohort the extra 34-week bill could reach tens of thousands of dollars across the season. Democratic member involvement helps absorb this through shared efficiency gains, but the wage floor now rises faster than the premium wine market is guaranteed to pass on, pressuring SBV's per-bottle economics on 120,000 units.

Input cost inflation (13.2% bottle glass and cork): Bottles and closures are a direct per-unit cost within the $9.60 variable cost. A 13.2% rise on glass and corks adds roughly $0.35–$0.50 per bottle — at 120,000 bottles that is about $42,000 to $60,000 a year, eroding the $7.20 contribution before any of the $1.20 single-vineyard premium is passed on, and arriving exactly as the barrel-maturation hall comes online and volumes rise.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in bottle glass and cork costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every bottle SBV fills — roughly $42,000 to $60,000 a year at 120,000 units — directly reducing the $7.20 contribution and colliding with a 13.2%-fuelled packaging budget for the hall launch; unlike the wage rise it cannot be offset by productivity, and unlike the interest rise it scales with every bottle sold. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious pressure and can be partly absorbed by the harvest-bonus retention saving on re-recruitment, while the interest-rate change is minor given SBV's equity-funded expansion; SBV should nevertheless lock in a bottle and cork supply contract or forward purchase before April 2027 to defend its margin.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SBV's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SBV with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
